text:
ROXANE (laughing):
  Since he is a cadet in your company!

CYRANO:
  Ah!...

ROXANE:
  He bears wit and genius upon his brow;
  He is proud, noble, young, intrepid, handsome...

CYRANO (rising, deathly pale):
  Handsome!

ROXANE:
  What? What is the matter with you?

CYRANO:
  With me, nothing... It is... it is...
  (He points to his hand, with a smile):
  It is this little hurt.

ROXANE:
  In short, I love him. Besides, I must tell you
  That I have never seen him except at the theater...

CYRANO:
  So you have not spoken to each other?

ROXANE:
  Only our eyes.

CYRANO:
  But how do you know, then?

ROXANE:
  Beneath the lindens
  Of the Place Royale, people talk... Some gossips
  Have informed me...

CYRANO:
  He is a cadet?

ROXANE:
  A cadet in the Guards.

CYRANO:
  His name?

ROXANE:
  Baron Christian de Neuvillette.

CYRANO:
  What?...
  He is not with the cadets.

ROXANE:
  Yes, since this morning:
  Captain Carbon de Castel-Jaloux.

CYRANO:
  Quickly,
  Quickly, one casts away one's heart!... But, my poor little one...

THE DUENNA (opening the door at the back):
  I have finished the cakes, Monsieur de Bergerac!

CYRANO:
  Well, then! Read the verses printed on the bag!
  (The duenna disappears):
  ...My poor child, you who love only fine speech,
  Wit—what if he were an uncultivated savage?

ROXANE:
  No, he has the hair of one of d'Urfé's heroes!

CYRANO:
  What if he were as ill-spoken as he is well-coiffed!

ROXANE:
  No, every word he says is refined—I can tell!

CYRANO:
  Yes, every word is refined when the mustache is fine.
  —But what if he were a fool!...

ROXANE (stamping her foot):
  Well! I would die of it, then and there!

CYRANO (after a pause):
  You had me come here to tell me that?
  I do not quite see the usefulness of it, madame.

ROXANE:
  Ah, it is because someone yesterday put death into my soul
  By telling me that all of you, all of you are Gascons
  In your company...

CYRANO:
  And that we challenge
  All the callow youths who, through favor, gain admission
  Among the pure Gascons that we are, without being Gascons themselves?
  Is that what you were told?

ROXANE:
  And you can imagine how
  I trembled for him!

CYRANO (between his teeth):
  Not without reason!

ROXANE:
  But I thought,
  When yesterday you appeared before us, invincible and great,
  Punishing that rogue, standing up to those brutes—
  I thought: if he were willing, he whom they will all fear...

CYRANO:
  Very well, I shall protect your little baron.

ROXANE:
  Oh! You will protect him for me, will you not?
  I have always felt such tender affection for you.

CYRANO:
  Yes, yes.

ROXANE:
  You will be his friend?

CYRANO:
  I shall.

ROXANE:
  And he will never have a duel?

CYRANO:
  I swear it.

ROXANE:
  Oh! I am very fond of you. I must go.
  (She quickly puts her mask back on, places a piece of lace over her brow, and,
  distractedly):
  But you have not told me about the battle
  Last night. Truly, it must have been unheard of!...
  —Tell him to write to me.
  (She blows him a little kiss from her hand):
  Oh! I love you!

CYRANO:
  Yes, yes.

ROXANE:
  A hundred men against you? Come, farewell.—We are
  Great friends!

CYRANO:
  Yes, yes.

ROXANE:
  Have him write to me!—A hundred men!—
  You will tell me later. Now, I cannot stay.
  A hundred men! What courage!

CYRANO (bowing to her):
  Oh! I have done better since then.
  (She exits. Cyrano remains motionless, his eyes lowered. A silence. The
  door on the right opens. Ragueneau puts his head through.)



Scene 2.VII.

Cyrano, Ragueneau, the poets, Carbon de Castel-Jaloux, the cadets, the
crowd, etc., then De Guiche.


RAGUENEAU:
  May we come back in?

CYRANO (without moving):
  Yes...
  (Ragueneau signals, and his friends come back in. At the same time, Carbon
  de Castel-Jaloux appears at the door at the back, in the uniform of a captain
  in the Guards, gesticulating broadly when he sees Cyrano.)

CARBON DE CASTEL-JALOUX:
  There he is!

CYRANO (raising his head):
  My captain!...

CARBON (exultantly):
  Our hero! We know everything! Some thirty
  Of my cadets are here!...

CYRANO (drawing back):
  But...

CARBON (trying to pull him along):
  Come! They want to see you!

CYRANO:
  No!

CARBON:
  They are drinking across the way, at the Croix du Trahoir.

CYRANO:
  I...

CARBON (going up to the door and shouting offstage in a voice of
  thunder):
  The hero refuses. He is in a surly mood!

A VOICE (outside):
  God's blood!
  (An uproar outside, the sound of swords and boots drawing nearer.)

CARBON (rubbing his hands):
  Here they come, crossing the street!

THE CADETS (entering the pastry shop):
  A thousand gods!—God's head!—God's death!—By God's head!

RAGUENEAU (recoiling in terror):
  Gentlemen, are you all from Gascony, then?

THE CADETS:
  All of us!

A CADET (to Cyrano):
  Bravo!

CYRANO:
  Baron!

ANOTHER (shaking his hands):
  Long live Cyrano!

CYRANO:
  Baron!

THIRD CADET:
  Let me embrace you!

CYRANO:
  Baron!...

SEVERAL GASCONS:
  Let us embrace him!

CYRANO (not knowing which one to answer):
  Baron!... baron!... please...

RAGUENEAU:
  Are you all barons, gentlemen?

THE CADETS:
  All?

RAGUENEAU:
  Are they?...

FIRST CADET:
  One could build a tower with our coronet bands alone!

LE BRET (entering and running to Cyrano):
  They are looking for you! A delirious crowd, led
  By those who walked behind you last night...

CYRANO (alarmed):
  You did not tell them where I am?...

LE BRET (rubbing his hands):
  Yes, I did!

A BURGHER (entering, followed by a group):
  Monsieur, the whole Marais is having itself carried here!
  (Outside, the street has filled with people. Sedan chairs and
  carriages draw up.)

LE BRET (softly, smiling, to Cyrano):
  And Roxane?

CYRANO (sharply):
  Be quiet!

THE CROWD (shouting outside):
  Cyrano!...
  (A mob surges into the pastry shop. Jostling. Cheers.)

RAGUENEAU (standing on a table):
  My shop
  Is overrun! They are breaking everything! It is magnificent!

PEOPLE (around Cyrano):
  My friend... my friend...

CYRANO:
  Yesterday I did not have
  So many friends!

LE BRET (delighted):
  Success!
